finalResponse:
# Notes Written Before Anyone Sees a Creative Route

*Deliberately before. The moment a repositioning acquires a manifesto film and a mood board, the question stops being "what is actually declining and why" and becomes "which of these three routes feels braver" — and the room will pick the brave one, and the brave one is the one that gets screenshotted.*

---

## The question I'd want re-asked before anything else

"Under-35 purchase share is declining every year." I'd want that number pulled apart before I accepted the brief it implies, because two entirely different diseases produce that same symptom and they take opposite treatments.

**Life-stage:** every generation has bought this brand at thirty-eight and not at twenty-eight. Under-35 share has always been low and always recovers as people acquire kitchens, mortgages, children, joint pain, whatever the category attaches to. In which case the recruitment engine is intact, the decline is arithmetic, and three modernisation campaigns have been fired at a phase of life.

**Cohort:** today's thirty-year-old buys materially less than the 2010 thirty-year-old did *at thirty*. In which case each cohort arrives lighter and never catches up, the base is being consumed rather than replenished, and we have maybe two decades of decline already banked regardless of what we do next.

One decomposition, penetration by age band by year, fifteen years, and we know which. I'd want it inside a fortnight and I'd want it before anybody briefs an agency, because the difference between the two answers is the difference between a repositioning and a patience exercise. My suspicion is it's both, in a ratio nobody has bothered to establish, and that a good part of what's being read as "seen as outdated" is a cohort that simply never encountered the product in a situation they were in.

And the third possibility, which is the one I'd bet has never been tested: **the brand isn't perceived as outdated, the purchase experience is.** If the product pages are 2012-grade, the reviews are thin, there's no small format for a one-person household, mobile checkout takes six screens and the only shelf we own is in a store format under-35s don't visit — then "outdated" is a report on our infrastructure, not our identity. It's worth knowing whether we've been redesigning a logo to fix a checkout.

---

## The mechanism of the last two failures, which I'd want stated out loud

Both backlashes had the same engine, and it wasn't change. It was **disavowal**.

Young consumers don't reject old brands. Workwear, hand tools, film cameras, vinyl, century-old vacuum flasks that turned up on TikTok — the culture is currently generous to anything with a verifiable past. What it punishes, without exception, is a brand claiming a youth identity it hasn't earned, in language it borrowed, about itself. Not oldness. Pretending.

The loyal base, symmetrically, isn't allergic to novelty. It's allergic to being told that what it has bought for thirty years was embarrassing. "Not your father's [brand]" insults both audiences in six words: it tells the young we're anxious and it tells the base they're the problem. Every previous route probably contained some polite version of that sentence.

So the design constraint is precise, and narrower than the fear in the room suggests: **we can change almost anything as long as we apologise for nothing.** Additive, never substitutive. Nothing retired with an announcement. No repositioning that requires the old brand to have been wrong.

The other half of the base problem isn't semiotic at all, it's mechanical. Long-loyal buyers are habit buyers; they navigate to us by colour block, silhouette and shape at a metre and a half in half a second, not by reading. Break the navigation furniture and volume drops — and that drop will be misread in the boardroom as "the base rejected our new values" when in fact they walked past us. I would like that misreading pre-empted in writing, because it will otherwise be used to shut down the entire programme.

---

## The asymmetry I'd build the whole thing on

There's exactly one asset class that both audiences read favourably, for opposite reasons, and it's the one previous campaigns tried to escape.

The base reads the archive as *continuity* — proof we haven't changed, reassurance their choice was sound. Under-35s read the same archive as *novelty* — an aesthetic they weren't present for, therefore fresh, and, crucially, unfakeable. A four-year-old DTC competitor can buy better packaging, better influencers and a better founder story. It cannot buy 1961.

So the direction of travel is not forward into youth. It is *deeper into ourselves, at a different volume, in different rooms*. That is also the only move available that doesn't require trading one audience against the other, and after two failures I'd want a strategy whose central mechanism is structurally incapable of producing the last outcome.

The conversion that has to happen is one word wide. Heritage is currently being used as **sentiment** — a claim about our past, addressed to people who share it, worthless to anyone who doesn't. It needs to become a **standard** — a claim about the product's present, legible to someone who has never heard of us. "Since 1954" is a fact about the company. "Still made the slow way, because the fast way is worse, and here's the side-by-side" is a fact about the thing in your hand. One is a plaque. The other is a reason to buy.

---

## The positioning

I'd write it so that both audiences can read it favourably without either being addressed, because the second we address the young explicitly we have re-run the failure.

**From:** the brand you inherited.
**To:** the brand that never got worse.

Longer, for internal use only, and never to appear in advertising: *seventy years of refusing the cheaper method — visible in the product, provable on request.*

Note what it does. To the base it says: *we haven't changed and we're not sorry.* To a twenty-six-year-old, in a category of shrinkflation, reformulation, private-label lookalikes and brands that are three years old and pretend to be forty, the identical sentence reads as integrity and mild defiance — which is the current currency. Same words, two readings, no bridging film required. **A repositioning that has to be explained to one of its audiences has already failed with the other.**

What this positioning explicitly refuses to be: purposeful, generational, conversational, self-aware. No values claim we can't evidence in the operations, because under-35s audit and the penalty for an unevidenced claim is far worse than the penalty for silence.

---

## Preserve versus retire — settled by measurement, not by taste

The internal disagreement is currently phrased as "how much change can the brand absorb," which is unanswerable, which is why it's still going. It's a question about volume when the real question is **location**. Some assets are load-bearing and some are merely old, and the difference is empirical.

The instrument is unglamorous: show each asset stripped of the name — colour alone, shape alone, mark alone, the sound, the tagline fragment, the pack silhouette — and measure how many people attribute it to us and only us. High attribution means load-bearing, regardless of whether anyone in the design review likes it. Low attribution means nobody will mourn what they can't recall.

I'd want that run before the debate resumes, because it converts a status contest into a data question, and status contests are won by whoever is most senior rather than most right.

My expectation of what it returns:

**Preserve, unconditionally** — the name, the primary colour, the pack silhouette, the mark in its recognisable form, the one manufacturing claim that is actually true and actually differentiating. These are the navigation furniture. They are also, awkwardly for everyone with a portfolio to build, the assets a designer most wants to fix.

**Free to move, continuously, no permission needed** — photography, secondary typography, layout, tone of voice, media choice, collaborations, pack formats and sizes, variants, the website in its entirety, everything that touches the purchase. This is the expression layer and it should be in permanent motion. The suspicion I'd raise gently: previous campaigns probably moved the identification assets and left the expression conservative, which is precisely backwards, and would explain both failures at once.

**Retire quietly, no announcement, no eulogy** — whatever the attribution test says nobody can recall. Anything self-congratulatory about longevity. Any device that positions the brand as a family inheritance, because that is the exact frame that tells a young buyer this isn't for them. Endline included, if it's a sentiment rather than a standard.

**Never touch** — the formulation, the specification, the thing the base's habit is actually attached to. If the product has to change to reach the young, we don't have a repositioning problem, we have a new product, and it should be sold under an adjacent name where its failure is survivable.

---

## Channels and content

The premise I'd argue for, and it constrains the budget shape considerably: **cultural relevance cannot be manufactured in channels we control.** Under-35 belief about brands is formed by other people talking, and a brand's own account is understood as advertising no matter how casually it's written. So we spend most of the effort on *supplying* the conversation and very little on *performing* in it.

**Open the archive properly.** Seventy years of advertising, packaging, factory film, catalogues, specification sheets, discontinued variants, the founder's correspondence if it exists. Digitised, high-resolution, licensed for reuse, searchable. This is cheap, it is a genuine competitive asset nobody can replicate, and it hands creators raw material rather than a message. It's also the single move that delights the base in the same instant.

**Process, at length, unedited-feeling.** Cameras on the making. Long, slow, unnarrated, no music bed. Process content is functionally immune to the inauthenticity charge because it isn't a claim, it's a fact with a lens pointed at it — and it is the exact content that converts heritage-as-sentiment into heritage-as-standard.

**Creators seeded, not briefed.** Paid, disclosed, and given the product plus access to the archive and the factory, then left alone. A brief is the tell. If we can't tolerate an unflattering line, we shouldn't be in the channel, and I'd accept a few uncomfortable posts as the honest price of the ones that land. Chosen for craft adjacency — people who care about how things are made — not for follower count, which buys reach we can already get more cheaply.

**Fix the buying, silently, first.** Product pages, reviews, small formats, subscription, marketplace presence, the shelf sets and store formats we're absent from. This is where the perception of "outdated" is probably manufactured, and none of it requires a single word of new brand communication.

**The base keeps traditional media, unchanged in tone and unchanged in weight.** Not reduced as the visible cost of the new work. And under no circumstances a multi-generational execution where the older person is charmingly bewildered — the trope is the insult, dressed as inclusion.

---

## Sequencing, which is where the backlash is actually prevented

The rule that governs the whole schedule: **change earns permission through evidence, and evidence arrives via product and third parties, never via announcement.** A campaign that declares a new era asks to be judged on intent before there is anything to judge — which is why it gets mocked. So we announce nothing. There is no launch. There is no reveal.

**Months 0–3, diagnosis, no external change.** Cohort/life-stage decomposition. Asset attribution. Occasion mapping: where an under-35 need in this category is currently being
